pages.description: Could piecing together how peasants lived more than two millennia ago change what we know?
pages.text: The secret lives of forgotten ancient Greeks | National Geographic By Candida Moss Published July 31, 2026 Stones & Bones is back! Today, we visit an excavation underway in Greece that may reshape what we know about its ancient past. Want to make sure you get every Stones & Bones newsletter? Put your email here . More than two millennia ago, young girls from the Greek countryside used to travel every four years to the Sanctuary of Artemis at Brauron outside Athens, to participate in a mysterious rite of passage. They went there, one ancient participant enigmatically said, to “play the bear.” Guided by the priestesses of Artemis and out of sight of their fathers and brothers, the girls ran free, embodying the bear as part of a ritual that allowed them to shed their wildness and prepare for marriage. Painted cups found at the site that were possibly made by participants themselves show girls running and dancing. They would return later in life to dedicate offerings to the goddess in preparation for childbirth. One day in the third century B.C., the sanctuary was abandoned forever. And no one knows why. Now, a team of British and Greek archaeologists, paleontologists, and other scientists jointly working as part of the ARTEMIS project want to understand not just what those girls were up to and why the sanctuary was abandoned but also what life in rural Brauron was really like for the ordinary inhabitants of ancient Greece. pages.description: The history of Paris is inextricably linked to the river that flows through its center—from Neolithic settlement to this year’s Olympic games.
pages.text: The Seine is at the center of the 2024 Olympics. Here's how the iconic river shaped Paris. | National Geographic By Mary Winston Nicklin Published July 16, 2024 When the 2024 Summer Olympics kick off in Paris, the city is going for the wow factor. The opening ceremony won’t take place in a stadium but—bucking tradition—outside on the River Seine. For the Parade of Nations, boats carrying the participating teams will glide by an estimated 300,000 spectators congregated on the quays. Bathed in myth and memory, the Seine is the lifeblood of the city that sprang up on its banks. Along this “main street,” as Napoleon called it, photogenic Pari­sian landmarks are on proud display, oozing grandeur and majesty. It’s so cen­tral to the city’s existence that building numbers are linked to the river: Those on perpendicular streets begin their num­bering closest to the Seine, while on parallel streets building numbers ascend in the direction of the current. “For Parisians, there’s a strong historical and visceral attachment to the river,” says Pierre Rabadan, the deputy mayor in charge of sport, the Olympic and Paralympic Games, and the Seine. ( Paris made an Olympic-size effort to clean up the Seine—did they succeed? ) The genesis of Paris From its source in Burgundy, the Seine flows 483 miles to reach the sea at Le Havre, with the capital sitting nearly in the middle. The River’s Parisian cartography has changed over time, its course altered by incessant floods, its branches and channels ultimately merging into the serpentine riverbed we know today. pages.text: The Treasures Emerging From Turkey’s Dying Lakes | National Geographic Premium HISTORY & CULTURE The Treasures Emerging From Turkey’s Dying Lakes Climate change is exposing once-submerged churches, castles and petroglyphs—and threatening their survival. The Basilica of Saint Neophytos, the likely site of early Christianity's Nicene Council, used to be submerged beneath Lake İznik. But drought has caused the lake's waters to recede, exposing the ancient structure. Sercan Ozkurnazl, Getty Images By Katie Nadworny Published September 24, 2026 Mustafa Şahin used to spend much more of his time below water. As the founder of Turkey’s first underwater archaeology department, he practiced his work in the country’s lakes, diving deep to uncover important historical ruins. In 2014, he found the Basilica of Saint Neophytos—a contender for the home of the original Nicene Council —in Lake İznik, a discovery that Archaeology Magazine and The Archaeological Institute of America deemed one of the most important that year. But Mustafa isn’t diving anymore. His work as head archaeologist of the basilica now keeps him out of the lake, because Saint Neophytos is no longer under İznik’s waters. It sits on dry ground. Lake İznik is facing a crisis and it isn’t alone. Turkey is losing most of its lakes at an alarming rate: close to 75 percent are in the process of disappearing, many within the last decade. How the Star-Spangled Banner became America's national anthem To celebrate their victory over British forces during the War of 1812, U.S. soldiers raised a large American flag at Fort McHenry in Baltimore, Maryland, on September 14, 1814. Poet Francis Scott Key was inspired by seeing the flag after witnessing the fort’s bombardment. He wrote a poem called "Defence of Fort M'Henry." This eventually became the Star-Spangled Banner and the United States national anthem. See the lyrics and learn more about the Star-Spangled Banner. Photograph by Reuben Wu, Nat Geo Image Collection By Theo Nicitopoulos Published November 15, 2024 In 1971, researchers made a surprising discovery while studying Greenland's ice: Temperatures over the island spiked by very large amounts within short periods thousands of years ago. The finding showed that abrupt warming could happen over just several decades and changed how they thought about natural climate change. ( Arctic Ice Isn't Doomed Yet—Here's How to Save It) Today, the world is the in the grips of another major shift, this time due to anthropogenic activities. And scientists are making predictions about how ice will soon evolve as temperatures warm. In a new study published today in the journal The Cryosphere , researchers modeled how much glaciers will melt by the year 2100. Representations of dogs, often in the form of gargoyles, can be spotted in Christian monuments across Europe. They symbolized various admirable qualities, including loyalty, domestic comfort, and protection. IVAN VDOVIN/ALAMY/CORDON PRESS By Monica Walker Vadillo Published October 24, 2025 In the second or third century A.D., an anonymous author in Alexandria, Egypt, composed a text entitled Physiologus, or The Naturalist. The work was soon widely copied and comprised of 48 or 49 chapters. Each was dedicated to a specific animal and included an illustration, a description of its characteristics, and a story—part natural observation, part imaginative anecdote—about its behavior. One such story, for example, features the lion. It was said that lion cubs were born lifeless and watched over by their mother until the father, king of the beasts, arrived and breathed life into them. Their build and claws have drawn comparisons to sloths, but some of these reptiles stood over 13 feet tall and weighed more than five tons. Back in 2012, paleontologists from the Mongolian Academy of Sciences initially unearthed parts of the spine, ribs, hips, and shoulders, and finally found two complete hands. Chang Lab / UCSF People with severe paralysis can struggle to communicate with others. While experimental brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) have come a long way in being able to help them convey their thoughts , these technologies have generally been limited to either speech or movement . Now, scientists have developed a tool that can do both simultaneously. The implant, described in the journal Nature Neuroscience on September 14, allows users to control the speech and movement of a virtual avatar with their mind in real time. pages.title: This Four-Person NASA Crew Spent Over a Year on 'Mars.' Here's What They Did for 378 Days in a Simulated Martian Habitat
pages.description: An intense selection process and long preparation helped set the crew up for cohabitation in a 3D-printed replication of the Red Planet's environment in Houston. There, they practiced Marswalks, disrupted communications with people on Earth and food cultivation
pages.text: This Four-Person NASA Crew Spent Over a Year on 'Mars.' Here's What They Did for 378 Days in a Simulated Martian Habitat Skip to main content Four individuals participated in NASA's second Crew Health and Performance Exploration Analog (CHAPEA) mission. NASA / James Blair On October 31, four NASA crewmembers returned from “Mars.” Not the actual Red Planet, of course, but a 3D-printed Mars habitat in Houston where the three men and one woman lived for 378 days. Now, the Mars analog astronauts— Ross Elder , Ellen Ellis , James Spicer and Matthew Montgomery —have started telling the world what took place after they disappeared into NASA’s Mars Dune Alpha habitat at the Johnson Space Center on October 19, 2025, for the agency’s second Crew Health and Performance Exploration Analog (CHAPEA) mission. The mission aimed to test the kinds of physical and mental conditions that a team of Mars explorers would endure on the Red Planet, including long-term isolation, disrupted communication with people on Earth and food cultivation. The habitat includes both a base and a mock outdoor environment , so the crew could practice Marswalks. “For more than a year, they have lived in an isolated environment, conducting critical research and helping us better understand what it will take to send humans to Mars,” Vanessa Wyche , director of NASA’s Johnson Space Center, said during a livestream , just before the crew emerged. “Inside just 1,700 square feet, they managed to live with limited resources. They maintained their habitat. They grew crops, and they carried out simulated Mars operations.”

pages.title: This Lollipop Could Help Blind Women Independently Detect Pregnancy
pages.description: Design student Sneha Rao is developing Tact, an edible pregnancy test that allows people with vision impairment to feel its results on their tongues
pages.text: This Lollipop Could Help Blind Women Independently Detect Pregnancy Skip to main content The user, if pregnant, will feel raised bumps on both sides of the flat lollipop—a reaction to hCG, a hormone that the body produces during pregnancy. TACT Sneha Rao, a 27-year-old master’s student in design at Carnegie Mellon University, can trace the inspiration for her invention back to a 2020 article in the Wall Street Journal . In it, Eleanor Southwood, then the chair of the Royal National Institute of Blind People , said, “The dream is to buy any pregnancy test with the knowledge that it’s accessible.” A few years later, Rao came across a Newsweek article that talked about Joanne Hewitson, a blind woman whose TikTok went viral in 2024. “She talked about never being able to take a pregnancy test alone,” says Rao. As most pregnancy tests available on the market provide visual results, Hewitson has to depend on her sister to read the results for her. Museum Wales In 1999, Peter Hughes stumbled upon the brass combination lock on Margam Beach in Wales. It featured four rotating dials, each bearing six letters. The dials turned smoothly, but only one of 1,296 possible combinations would open the device. The lock was an artifact from the Ann Francis , a merchant ship that sank in 1583. Hundreds of the vessel’s treasures—including compasses, coins and cannonballs—have since surfaced on the beach. But Hughes was particularly intrigued by the lock. He fiddled with the dials for two decades, trying to solve the puzzle. Now, researchers have used CT scans to reveal the four-letter code: ANCE. According to a parish register, 14 sailors died in December 1583, and these men may have been the Ann Francis ’ crew. pages.text: This Odd-Looking New Spinosaurus Is Reviving an Age-Old Debate | National Geographic SCIENCE This Odd-Looking New Spinosaurus Is Reviving an Age-Old Debate Could Spinosaurus swim? A new fossil with a scimitar-like head crest provides new evidence on the unsettled question. Unearthed in a rare Saharan fossil site in Niger, Spinosaurus mirabilis had a large head crest that may have signaled a message to rivals competing for resources or territory along the way. artwork by Dani Navarro By Helen Thompson Published February 19, 2026 Under the central Saharan sun, paleontologist Daniel Vidal spotted a mysterious bone poking out of the ground during an excavation in Niger. It looked like a dinosaur vertebra at first. But upon further inspection, researchers realized the bone was a curved, sword-like crest that would have been attached to the skull of one of paleontology’s most oddball dinosaurs—the sail-backed predator Spinosaurus . “It was amazing,” recalls Vidal, of the University of Chicago. “It was like a unicorn.” Back in 2022, when he stumbled upon the strange bone, he was part of a team led by National Geographic Explorer Paul Sereno, a paleontologist also at Chicago , excavating a remote fossil site called Jenguebi. Now, the researchers report the crest belonged to an entirely new species— Spinosaurus mirabilis —that roamed the area’s ancient river ecosystem some 95 million years ago in the Late Cretaceous. They published their discovery Thursday in Science . The new species adds to a heated debate over how these puzzling (and popular) dinosaurs lived and hunted in water.

The harbour wall of Lyme Regis is also known as The Cobb. Thomas Faull, Getty Images By Jessica Prupas Published August 1, 2026 This article was produced by National Geographic Traveller (UK). Were you to dig below Lyme Regis’ bunting-slung streets, you’d hit a geological marvel: the Blue Lias. This vast sequence of limestone and shale layers, formed during the Mesozoic era some 200 million years ago, reveals fossils as it erodes, making the town one of Europe’s most important paleontological centres. It’s a badge locals wear proudly: you’ll find a weather-beaten statue of celebrated fossil hunter Mary Anning overlooking Church Cliff Beach. In 1823, while wandering Lyme Regis’s coastline, she unearthed the world’s first complete skeleton of a Plesiosaurus and, nearly two centuries after her death, the town remains a magnet for excavators. pages.text: Tracking a Mystery: When and How the First Americans Arrived | National Geographic The Oregon Coast, pictured here, may have been a byway for the first Americans as they followed the nutrient-rich coast southward on foot and by boat, says the new book, Atlas of a Lost World . Photograph by Ty Milford, Aurora BOOK TALK When, How Did the First Americans Arrive? It’s Complicated. The first Americans weren't one group of people; they arrived at different times, and likely by different methods. By Simon Worrall Published June 9, 2018 • 13 min read How did human beings first come to North America? Across the Bering Strait, on foot? Down the “kelp highway” by boat? Across the Atlantic via the polar ice cap? And when did they reach here? 10,000 years ago? 40,000? Or were they always here, as the Navajo and other Native American tribes believe? In his new book, Atlas Of A Lost World , author Craig Childs sets off to test these different theories on the ground, traveling from Alaska to Chile, Canada to Florida. What he finds, despite the best efforts of archaeologists and the latest technology , still remains in many ways a mystery. Speaking from his home in Colorado, he explains why many Native Americans reject the idea that their ancestors migrated from somewhere else; how an archaeologist nicknamed Dr. Poop believes he has identified the first human excrement in America ; and why diversity seems to have been built into America’s DNA. Trouble Funk: Tiny Desk Concert May 30, 2018 12:00 PM ET By Abby O'Neill Credit: NPR Go-go — Washington D.C.'s regional twist on funk — reigned in the DMV during the 1980s, and one of the scene's signature acts was Trouble Funk. More than 30 years later, the collective, led by Big Tony Fisher, still fills sold-out venues with heavyweight percussion and call-and-response lyrics. Trouble Funk concerts are bona fide jam sessions, so I was determined to squeeze their unrelenting rhythms behind the Tiny Desk. With 12 members sandwiched into a cramped space, the electricity was almost tangible as they launched into the 1982 banger "Pump Me Up," a song sampled in Public Enemy's protest anthem "Fight the Power" and M/A/R/R/S's dance classic "Pump Up The Volume." The drum breaks here are definitive go-go and it was hard to discern who was having more fun: the band or the audience. On "Grip It," buoyant and staccato horn melodies propelled the song forward, while "Let's Get Small" featured Trouble Funk's classic call-and-response chants. "Drop the Bomb," another notable gem from their lengthy discography, kept the energy level high and "Don't Touch That Stereo" was all raw, unencumbered funk. pages.title: Two Centuries After This Bronze Leg Emerged From a Scottish Bog, Archaeologists Believe It May Have Belonged to a Towering Statue of a Roman Emperor on Horseback
pages.description: Long thought to have been looted from northern England by Scottish tribes, the larger-than-life leg may have actually been displayed in Roman Scotland, before it was carefully dismantled and buried by retreating forces
pages.text: Two Centuries After This Bronze Leg Emerged From a Scottish Bog, Archaeologists Believe It May Have Belonged to a Towering Statue of a Roman Emperor on Horseback Skip to main content Curator Fraser Hunter examines the bronze leg. Duncan McGlynn In 1820, a larger-than-life gilded bronze lower leg was pulled out of a bog in the Scottish Borders region. For more than two centuries, historians discredited the idea that the Roman-era artifact came from Scotland, instead assuming that it was hacked off a monument in England and hauled north by marauding tribes. But ahead of “ Roman Scotland: Life on the Edge of Empire ,” an exhibition at the National Museum of Scotland (NMS), researchers have determined that the so-called “Milsington leg” was not stolen from the south, nor was it violently severed. Instead, they posit that it formed part of a colossal equestrian statue of the Roman Emperor Antoninus Pius that once stood in southern Scotland in the second century C.E., before it was dismantled by retreating Roman troops. “This really turns on its head our understanding of Rome’s second attempt at conquering Scotland,” Fraser Hunter , principal curator of prehistoric and Roman archaeology at NMS, says in a statement . The bronze leg shows no signs of being violently hacked off the larger statue. National Museums Scotland Roman campaigns into modern-day Scotland began in the 70s C.E., several decades after the conquest of Britain . Common Name : Tyrannosaurus rex Scientific Name : Tyrannosaurus rex Type : Prehistoric Animals Diet : Carnivore Size : 40 feet long and 12 feet tall Weight : Between 5.5 and eight tons Size relative to a bus : Tyrannosaurus rex was one of the most ferocious predators to ever walk the Earth. With a massive body, sharp teeth, and jaws so powerful they could crush a car, this famous carnivore dominated the forested river valleys in western North America during the late Cretaceous period, 68 million years ago. Although T. rex is a household name, what we know about this tyrannosaur is constantly evolving. Improved technologies, such as biomechanical modeling and x-ray imaging, have allowed scientists to gain a deeper understanding of how this apex predator lived. Strengths Tyrannosaurus rex , whose name means “ king of the tyrant lizards ,” was built to rule. This dinosaur’s muscular body stretched as long as 40 feet—about the size of a school bus —from its snout to the tip of its powerful tail. Weighing up to eight tons, T. rex stomped headfirst across its territory on two strong legs. These dinosaurs likely preyed on living animals and scavenged carcasses —and sometimes they even ate one another . The head of a T. rex was the real stuff of nightmares. U.S. Energy Information Administration (EIA) About The Energy Information Administration (EIA) is a semi-independent agency under the U.S. Department of Energy and is the nation’s premier source for impartial energy information. By collecting, analyzing and sharing information on renewable energy, petroleum, natural gas, alternative fuels, and more, EIA helps policymakers and industry stakeholders make informed, data-driven decisions. To protect EIA’s independence and the public’s trust in their findings, EIA’s data, analyses, and forecasts are not approved or signed off on by any other officer or employee of the U.S. government.
